source.title: Double descent for least-squares interpolation on contaminated data: A simulation study

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Figures are not rendered, but their results are often described in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The study directly sweeps predictor count and reports test MSE shapes, but uses simulated linear regression rather than deep networks and evaluates contaminated-data settings as well as clean ones.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own test-MSE results for sweeps over p. Rows below capture those results, using the prose descriptions where available. Related-work claims are citations, not study results. Training-MSE, coefficient-difference, and iteration plots are omitted because they do not measure the test-error curves named in the versions.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps predictor count p for linear-regression estimators and reports mean test MSE over 500 simulations. Its own results bear on whether risk falls again past the interpolation point (V4), in a new setting: clean versus X- or Y-contaminated training data. There are no deep networks, epoch sweeps, regularization tuning or complexity recounting.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, with two corrections. The authors find the minimum l2-norm interpolator shows double descent (minimum at p=s, peak at p=n, descent after) at SNR of at least 2, and it generalizes better than all robust alternatives across settings. Under Y-contamination there is only a post-peak descent, which they say is not double descent. Huber-loss and RRBoost-based interpolation show similar double descent on clean or mildly contaminated data. Tukey, SLTS-based interpolation, raw SLTS and raw RRBoost do not. The record wrongly groups RRBoost-based interpolation with those that fail.
record.recipe_differences: The study sweeps predictor count and measures test MSE, but uses simulated linear regression rather than deep networks; it varies contamination, design, SNR, and estimator. Results are mean test MSE over 500 simulations.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported curve shapes vary with SNR, contamination type and radius, training sample size, predictor centering, covariance design, contamination magnitude, and estimator. The paper notes that the Huber peak can shift with contamination radius.

fits_no_version.finding: Non-interpolating robust estimators (Tukey loss, raw SLTS, raw RRBoost) show flat or slightly rising test MSE with p and no double descent.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Double descent requires the estimator to actually interpolate the training data; bounded-influence or trimmed estimators that never interpolate show no second descent.

fits_no_version.finding: For Huber interpolation the peak moves to larger p with X-contamination, and the second descent starts roughly when training error vanishes (Sec. 6.1.2, 9.1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The peak location follows where training error reaches zero, not p=n.

fits_no_version.finding: Under Y-contamination, test MSE at p=5000 is larger for ntrain=200 than for ntrain=50 (Sec. 5.4.1). This is far from the threshold and the comparison is uncontrolled.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: More training data can raise test error deep in the overparameterized regime under label contamination.

record.code_released: https://github.com/shaobo-li/MTE (implementation package cited for Huber optimization); study simulation code release not stated
record.problems: The evidence is simulation-based and the reported uncertainty around mean test MSE is not stated. Most curve outcomes are visual or qualitative, and several plots are not rendered in the supplied text. The design is linear regression, not deep networks.
record.rows_left_out: More test-MSE plots are presented for spiked covariance, non-centered predictors (µ = 5), and additional estimator/contamination combinations (Secs. 5.2–5.5, Figs. 15–40). These are omitted to stay concise because the paper says their curves generally resemble the independent-feature cases already recorded, except for specific differences described in the text. Training-error, coefficient-difference, and iteration results (Secs. 6–8, Figs. 41–130) are omitted because they are not test-error measurements.

untested.parts: No deep networks; linear regression only.
No sweep over epochs or training time.
There is no controlled sample-size sweep near the interpolation threshold. n=50 and n=200 are compared only under Y-contamination, at large p.
Only linear-regression estimators are tested (minimum-norm, Huber, subset-based interpolators). Neural networks, kernels and trees are not.
No effective-complexity measure is used across axes. The paper only notes that Huber's second descent starts roughly when training error vanishes.
There is no noise-free baseline and no peak-height-versus-noise comparison. Optimally tuned regularization and multiple descent are not tested.
No recounting of complexity by an effective number of parameters.

missing.what: Huber interpolation, Y-contamination, cout=10000. For r in {0.1,0.25}: minimum at p=s, then MSE increases monotonically with no descent. For r≥0.5: peak near p=2000. rows_left_out wrongly treats this as resembling the recorded cases.
Huber interpolation with µ=5: no clear peak on clean or X-contaminated data. MSE increases with p for Y-contamination at r=0.1 and 0.25.
Minimum-norm interpolator with µ=5 and Y-contamination: after the peak, MSE stays near small-p values, a weak second descent.
Spiked covariance: shapes resemble the independent design, but MSE is higher and final large-p MSE is much higher under contamination.

record.verdict_notes: Results are qualitative descriptions of unrendered figures, with no uncertainty reported. Rows on minimum-norm interpolation reproduce a known linear-regression double descent; the new contribution is the contamination setting. V6 links were removed throughout because SNR and contamination are varied but the peak's dependence on noise is not isolated.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses linear regression, not deep networks.
No sweep over training epochs or training time.
The study varies ntrain across scenarios, but does not report a controlled test of whether adding training samples near the interpolation threshold raises test error.
The study examines simulated linear regression estimators, not a broad range of distinct model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is proposed or tested as predicting peak location across axes.
The study varies SNR and contamination, but does not test optimally tuned regularization or multiple/triple descent.
No re-counting of complexity using an effective number of parameters.

rows.subject: Huber-loss interpolation

conditions.value: r = 0.1: peak at p = 100; r = 0.5: peak shifted to p = 500

rows.value: The peak shifts to the right as r increases; test-MSE values at low and large p are comparable with clean-data values.
rows.note: The change in peak location with contamination radius is stated explicitly.
rows.check: Drop V6. The second descent is present; the peak shifts from p=100 to p=500 as r rises, tracking where training error vanishes. Low-p and high-p MSE match clean data, so this is not a weakening.

source_check.correct: Peak locations p=100 at r=0.1 and p=500 at r=0.5 are explicitly stated. Full double descent is qualified by sufficiently large SNR in Sec. 9.1; restrict the observed state accordingly or split the row by SNR.

rows.subject: Tukey-loss interpolation

conditions.value: peak at p = 20 when SNR > 1; otherwise peak at p = n or curves nearly constant

rows.value: Where a peak occurs, curves increase before it and briefly decrease before becoming constant; for low SNR curves are nearly constant.

rows.subject: SLTS-based interpolation
rows.operation_detail: Swept predictor count p and measured mean test MSE over B = 500 simulations.
rows.value: MSE is much higher at low p, peaks at p = 20, and decreases clearly afterwards to values comparable to other scenarios at p = 5000.
rows.note: The text does not describe an initial decrease before the peak.
